issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: David, a 32-year-old North American male and park ranger, has been struggling with debilitating symptoms following a horrific experience of torture. The trauma left deep scars both physically and emotionally, profoundly affecting his daily life. The event that David endured was searingly vivid in some moments but entirely blank in others. He could recall the intense fear and pain as if it were yesterday, yet he struggled to form a coherent narrative around it. When trying to explain what happened, David often lost track of his thoughts, making it almost impossible for him to articulate the details coherently. David had come to believe that his body was permanently damaged by the torture, leaving him with a sense of physical vulnerability that persisted long after the event. This belief was reinforced every time he felt an intense bodily response before he could even process what was happening around him. His heart would race and his muscles would tense at the slightest hint of danger or discomfort, as if his body were always on high alert. David's fear of going crazy was a constant companion. He was certain that his exaggerated reactions post-trauma indicated a deep-seated mental instability. This belief made it challenging for him to trust others and rely on them for support. Instead, he found solace in rehearsing conversations before any interaction, meticulously planning every word to prevent the risk of saying something out of place. The fear of driving or being a passenger in a vehicle was another significant issue for David. The trauma had left him with an intense aversion to being enclosed and moving at high speeds, leading him to avoid these situations altogether. This avoidance extended to his daily life as a park ranger. He would often walk long distances instead of using a vehicle, which made his work more arduous and time-consuming. David's tendency to numb his feelings was another maladaptive strategy he had developed. Whenever the memories of the torture began to surface, he would retreat into emotional numbness, detaching from both his surroundings and himself. This numbing allowed him to continue functioning in his daily life but came at a steep cost, as it prevented him from fully engaging with others or experiencing joy. David's heightened sense of threat was also palpable. He assumed that any delay in routine activities was a sign of impending danger. For instance, if he expected someone to arrive and they were even slightly late, his mind would immediately jump to the worst-case scenario. This pattern extended to checking doors and windows repeatedly, ensuring that everything was secure multiple times before feeling at ease. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has been profound. David's relationships have suffered as a result of his avoidance and emotional detachment. His work as a park ranger became increasingly challenging due to his reluctance to use vehicles, which affected his ability to perform some essential duties efficiently. It wasn't until he realized that his life had become so restricted by fear and avoidance that he finally decided to seek help. What frightened him most was the prospect of continuing in this state indefinitely, unable to trust others or enjoy life fully. He hoped that with professional support, he could regain a sense of control over his thoughts and emotions and live more freely without the constant threat looming over him.
